explain.title: Probability
explain.body: “Probability is the chance of occurrence of a particular event.” It is calculated using P(A) = n(A)/n(S), where n(A) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) is the total number of possible outcomes.

explain.title: Experiment, outcomes, and sample space
explain.body: “The process which generates results e.g., tossing a coin, rolling a dice, etc. is called an experiment.” “The results of an experiment are called outcomes.” “The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called sample space.” The textbook denotes the sample space by S.

explain.title: Favourable outcome and event

explain.title: Probability limits and event types

explain.title: Sample space and sample point
explain.body: The sample space is the collection of all possible outcomes of an experiment. Each individual outcome in it is a sample point. For three coin tosses, the sample space has eight outcomes.

explain.title: Probability of an event
explain.body: When outcomes are equally likely, probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. For a pair of dice there are 36 ordered outcomes, and only one is double 2, so its probability is 1/36.

explain.title: Events that are not wanted
explain.body: For an event described with “not”, count outcomes outside the event. For example, the cards that are neither jacks nor kings are the other 44 cards in a 52-card pack, so the probability is 44/52 = 11/13.

explain.title: Relative frequency
explain.body: Relative frequency compares the observed frequency of an event with the total number of trials. Divide each frequency by the total frequency; the relative frequencies for all categories together add to 1.

explain.title: Expected frequency
explain.body: Expected frequency is the expected number of times an event occurs in a fixed number of trials. Multiply the probability of the event by the number of trials.

notes.title: Finding the Probability of an Event
notes.answer: P(A) = n(A)/n(S), the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes.
notes.explanation: Probability measures the chance that an event occurs. Your textbook defines it as: “Probability is the chance of occurrence of a particular event.” Use P(A) = n(A)/n(S), where n(A) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(S) is the total number of possible outcomes. For example, on one fair die, the probability of rolling a 6 is 1/6. When two dice are rolled, there are 36 possible ordered outcomes; the probability of getting an even number on both is 9/36 = 1/4.
notes.simple: Count the results you want, then divide by the total number of possible results. For example, a fair die has one 6 and six possible results, so the chance of rolling a 6 is 1/6.
examples: Two fair dice: P(even numbers on both) = 9/36 = 1/4.

List or count the favourable outcomes for event A.
Use P(A) = n(A)/n(S).
Simplify the fraction.

notes.title: Probability of an Event Not Occurring
notes.explanation: For any event, its complement means that the event does not happen. Find the event’s probability first, then subtract it from 1. For example, if getting a 6 has probability 1/6, not getting a 6 has probability 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. If the sum of two dice is 8 with probability 5/36, the probability that the sum is not 8 is 1 − 5/36 = 31/36.
notes.simple: To find the probability that an event does not happen, subtract the probability that it does happen from 1.
examples: A coin has P(head) = 1/2, so P(not head) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.

notes.answer: Use P(A) = n(A)/n(S) for equally likely outcomes, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A) for the complement.

For example, if a dice has 6 sides and 2 sides show a desired result, the probability is 2/6 = 1/3. If the probability of passing is 0.85, the probability of not passing is 1 − 0.85 = 0.15.

notes.title: Relative Frequency as an Estimate of Probability
notes.answer: Relative frequency = Frequency of specific event / Total frequency = x/N, where N = Σf
notes.explanation: Relative frequency shows how often an event occurred out of all the trials. Add all the frequencies to find the total, then divide the event’s frequency by that total.
notes.simple: Count how many times the event happened, then divide by the total number of times you tried.
examples: If the value 6 occurred 10 times in 43 trials, its relative frequency is 10/43 = 0.23.
If the value 8 occurred 2 times in 43 trials, its relative frequency is 2/43 = 0.04.
steps: Add the frequencies: Σf = 3 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 10 + 8 + 2 = 43.
For X = 6, divide its frequency by the total: 10/43 = 0.23.
For X = 8, divide its frequency by the total: 2/43 = 0.04.

notes.title: Finding relative frequency
notes.answer: Relative frequency = frequency of the outcome / total frequency.
notes.explanation: Relative frequency tells us how often an outcome happened compared with the total number of observations. It is used as an estimated probability.
notes.simple: Divide the number for the outcome you want by the total number of observations.
examples: If 45 out of 200 students do not play any game, their relative frequency is 45/200 = 0.225.
If 80 out of 200 students play cricket, the relative frequency is 80/200 = 0.4.

notes.title: Finding Expected Frequency
notes.explanation: Expected frequency tells us how many times an event should occur, on average, in a stated number of trials. Multiply the total number of trials by the probability of the event.
notes.simple: Expected frequency is the number of times an outcome is expected to happen. Multiply how many trials there are by the probability of that outcome.
examples: If an event has probability 0.2 in 50 trials, its expected frequency is 50 × 0.2 = 10.
For the outcome of 3 sixes in Example 11, the expected frequency is 50 × 0.24 = 12.
steps: Identify the total number of trials, N.
Identify the probability of the event, P(A).
Use Expected frequency = N × P(A).
Multiply and write the expected frequency.

notes.title: Expected Frequency
notes.answer: Expected frequency = number of trials × probability of the event.
notes.explanation: Expected frequency tells us how many times an event is likely to happen in a fixed number of trials. Use E(B) = N × P(B), where N is the number of trials and P(B) is the probability of the event. For example, if P(B) = 1/3 in 300 trials, E(B) = 300 × 1/3 = 100. If an item is either defective or non-defective, then P(non-defective) = 1 − P(defective).
notes.simple: Expected frequency is the number of times an event is likely to happen in a given number of trials.
examples: A fair die is rolled 300 times. The probability of getting 1 or 6 is 2/6 = 1/3, so the expected frequency is 300 × 1/3 = 100.
steps: Find the probability of the event.
Multiply the probability by the total number of trials: E(B) = N × P(B).
Write the expected frequency, and round only if the question or textbook does so.

For experimental data, divide each frequency by the total number of trials to find relative frequency. Expected frequency is found by multiplying the probability by the number of trials.

If 17 of 25 items are non-defective, their relative frequency is 17/25 = 0.68.
